questions.correct_answer: IaaS: manage OS and above; PaaS: manage app and data only; SaaS: just use the software
questions.explanation: IaaS=VM, PaaS=Azure SQL, SaaS=Power BI — each shifts more management to Microsoft.

questions.question_text: Azure SQL Database vs SQL Server on a VM — key difference:
choices: Azure SQL DB is fully managed PaaS (no patching); SQL on VM is IaaS (you manage OS and SQL)
questions.correct_answer: Azure SQL DB is fully managed PaaS (no patching); SQL on VM is IaaS (you manage OS and SQL)
questions.explanation: PaaS removes infrastructure management; IaaS gives full control at the cost of more responsibility.

questions.question_text: Azure Blob Storage vs Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 — ADLS Gen2 adds:
choices: A hierarchical namespace (folder structure) optimised for big data analytics
questions.correct_answer: A hierarchical namespace (folder structure) optimised for big data analytics
questions.explanation: ADLS Gen2 = Blob + hierarchical namespace + POSIX permissions = ideal for analytics workloads.

questions.question_text: Azure Data Factory (ADF) is primarily used for:
choices: Cloud ETL/ELT — orchestrating data movement and transformation pipelines
questions.correct_answer: Cloud ETL/ELT — orchestrating data movement and transformation pipelines
questions.explanation: ADF is the cloud equivalent of SSIS — 90+ connectors, serverless, scalable.

questions.question_text: Azure Synapse Analytics is best described as:
choices: A unified analytics platform combining SQL pools, Spark pools, pipelines, and Power BI integration
questions.correct_answer: A unified analytics platform combining SQL pools, Spark pools, pipelines, and Power BI integration
questions.explanation: Synapse combines data warehousing, big data, and BI in one integrated workspace.

questions.question_text: Azure Blob Storage supports a hierarchical folder namespace by default.
questions.explanation: Standard Blob Storage has a flat namespace; ADLS Gen2 adds the hierarchical namespace.

questions.question_text: Which Azure service is the cloud equivalent of SSIS?
questions.explanation: ADF replaces SSIS for cloud-native ETL/ELT pipelines.

questions.question_text: IaaS stands for Infrastructure as a ___.
questions.explanation: IaaS provides virtualised computing infrastructure over the internet.

questions.question_text: Azure Synapse SQL Pool is used for:
choices: Massively parallel processing (MPP) SQL queries on large-scale data warehouses
questions.correct_answer: Massively parallel processing (MPP) SQL queries on large-scale data warehouses
questions.explanation: Dedicated SQL Pool in Synapse is the distributed data warehouse engine.

questions.question_text: Azure SQL Database automatically handles patching and backups.
questions.explanation: As a PaaS service, Azure SQL DB manages patching, backups, and HA automatically.

questions.question_text: Which storage tier in Azure Blob is cheapest for rarely accessed archival data?
questions.explanation: Archive tier has the lowest storage cost but highest retrieval latency and cost.

questions.question_text: Azure Active Directory (Entra ID) is used in Azure for:
choices: Identity and access management — authentication and authorisation for Azure resources
questions.correct_answer: Identity and access management — authentication and authorisation for Azure resources
questions.explanation: Entra ID (AAD) is the identity backbone for all Azure security and access control.

questions.question_text: Azure Data Factory can connect to on-premises SQL Server using a Self-Hosted Integration Runtime.
questions.explanation: The Self-Hosted IR runs on your on-prem network, allowing ADF to reach local systems securely.

questions.question_text: Which Azure service would you use to run Apache Spark workloads?
choices: Azure Databricks or Azure Synapse Spark Pool
questions.correct_answer: Azure Databricks or Azure Synapse Spark Pool
questions.explanation: Both Databricks and Synapse provide managed Apache Spark environments.

questions.question_text: Resource Group in Azure is used to:
choices: Logically group related Azure resources for management, billing, and access control
questions.correct_answer: Logically group related Azure resources for management, billing, and access control
questions.explanation: Resource Groups are the primary organisational unit in Azure for managing related resources together.

questions.question_text: What are the four main components of an ADF Pipeline?
questions.explanation: Linked Services connect to data stores; Datasets point to data; Activities do the work; Pipelines orchestrate.

questions.question_text: A Linked Service in ADF is equivalent to:
choices: A connection string/credential to an external data source or compute
questions.correct_answer: A connection string/credential to an external data source or compute
questions.explanation: Linked Services define HOW to connect; Datasets define WHAT data within that connection.

questions.question_text: ADF vs SSIS — when would you choose ADF over SSIS?
choices: Cloud-native workloads, 90+ connectors, serverless scale, no infrastructure to manage
Complex on-prem transformations with rich UI
questions.correct_answer: Cloud-native workloads, 90+ connectors, serverless scale, no infrastructure to manage
questions.explanation: ADF excels in the cloud; SSIS is better for complex on-prem transformations.

questions.question_text: Delta Lake provides what key capabilities over plain Parquet?
choices: ACID transactions, time travel (versioning), schema enforcement, and upsert support
questions.correct_answer: ACID transactions, time travel (versioning), schema enforcement, and upsert support
questions.explanation: Delta Lake adds reliability and governance features that raw Parquet files lack.

questions.question_text: The Medallion Architecture layers are:
questions.explanation: Medallion is the standard Lakehouse pattern — progressively refining data quality.

questions.question_text: An ADF Copy Activity can move data from Azure Blob to Azure SQL Database.
questions.explanation: Copy Activity supports 90+ source and sink combinations including Blob to SQL.

questions.question_text: An ADF Schedule Trigger runs a pipeline:
choices: On a defined date/time recurrence — e.g. daily at 2am
questions.correct_answer: On a defined date/time recurrence — e.g. daily at 2am
questions.explanation: Schedule Trigger fires on a calendar cadence; Storage Event Trigger fires on file arrival.

questions.question_text: In Azure Databricks, code is written in ___ notebooks using Python, SQL, or Scala.
questions.explanation: ADB notebooks are Jupyter-compatible and support multiple languages.

questions.question_text: Delta Lake time travel allows you to:
choices: Query previous versions of a table using VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF
questions.correct_answer: Query previous versions of a table using VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF
questions.explanation: Delta maintains a transaction log enabling point-in-time queries and rollback.

questions.question_text: ADF Data Flows allow you to transform data visually without writing code.
questions.explanation: Mapping Data Flows provide a code-free transformation UI that runs on Spark.

questions.question_text: A Tumbling Window Trigger in ADF is used for:
choices: Processing data in fixed non-overlapping time intervals — e.g. hourly batches
questions.correct_answer: Processing data in fixed non-overlapping time intervals — e.g. hourly batches
questions.explanation: Tumbling Window ensures every interval is processed exactly once with backfill support.

questions.question_text: Azure Databricks clusters can be:
choices: Interactive (always on for notebooks) or Job clusters (start/stop per job run)
questions.correct_answer: Interactive (always on for notebooks) or Job clusters (start/stop per job run)
questions.explanation: Job clusters terminate after the job, saving cost; Interactive clusters stay up for exploration.

questions.question_text: In ADF, a Dataset must be associated with a Linked Service.
questions.explanation: A Dataset defines the data location within a connection defined by a Linked Service.

questions.question_text: Bronze layer in Medallion Architecture stores:
choices: Raw, unmodified data as-is from source systems
questions.correct_answer: Raw, unmodified data as-is from source systems
questions.explanation: Bronze is the landing zone — preserve source data exactly as received for auditability.

questions.question_text: Schema enforcement in Delta Lake means:
choices: Writes that don't match the table schema are rejected automatically
questions.correct_answer: Writes that don't match the table schema are rejected automatically
questions.explanation: Delta enforces schema on write, preventing data corruption from bad-format incoming data.

questions.question_text: What is the main advantage of Apache Spark over Hadoop MapReduce?
choices: Spark processes data in-memory, making it up to 100x faster than disk-based MapReduce
Spark is older and more mature
questions.correct_answer: Spark processes data in-memory, making it up to 100x faster than disk-based MapReduce
questions.explanation: In-memory processing eliminates the disk I/O bottleneck of MapReduce's write-between-stages model.

questions.question_text: HDFS stores data by:
choices: Splitting files into 128MB blocks distributed across nodes, replicated 3x for fault tolerance
Keeping one copy on one server
questions.correct_answer: Splitting files into 128MB blocks distributed across nodes, replicated 3x for fault tolerance
questions.explanation: Replication ensures data survives node failures; distribution enables parallel processing.

questions.question_text: What is an RDD in Spark?
choices: Resilient Distributed Dataset — immutable, fault-tolerant, partitioned collection of records
questions.correct_answer: Resilient Distributed Dataset — immutable, fault-tolerant, partitioned collection of records
questions.explanation: RDD is the foundational data structure of Spark — low-level but flexible.

questions.question_text: Transformations vs Actions in Spark:
choices: Transformations are lazy (build a plan); Actions trigger execution (count, show, write)
Actions are lazy; Transformations execute immediately
questions.correct_answer: Transformations are lazy (build a plan); Actions trigger execution (count, show, write)
questions.explanation: Spark's lazy evaluation optimises the execution plan before any computation occurs.

questions.question_text: Partitioning in Spark is important because:
choices: Good partitioning avoids expensive shuffles and enables parallel execution across nodes
questions.correct_answer: Good partitioning avoids expensive shuffles and enables parallel execution across nodes
questions.explanation: Poor partitioning causes data skew and shuffle bottlenecks — the #1 Spark performance issue.

questions.question_text: A Spark DataFrame has a defined schema, unlike an RDD.
questions.explanation: DataFrames are structured with named columns and types; RDDs are untyped collections.

questions.question_text: Hive in the Hadoop ecosystem provides:
choices: SQL-like interface (HQL) to query data stored in HDFS
questions.correct_answer: SQL-like interface (HQL) to query data stored in HDFS
questions.explanation: Hive translates SQL queries into MapReduce or Spark jobs on HDFS data.

questions.question_text: Spark's ___ evaluation means transformations are not executed until an action is called.
questions.explanation: Lazy evaluation allows Spark to optimise the full execution plan before running.

questions.question_text: A shuffle in Spark occurs when:
choices: Data must be redistributed across partitions — e.g. during joins or groupBy
questions.correct_answer: Data must be redistributed across partitions — e.g. during joins or groupBy
questions.explanation: Shuffles are expensive — they involve network I/O between executors.

questions.question_text: YARN is Hadoop's resource manager that allocates cluster resources to applications.
questions.explanation: YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator) manages CPU and memory across the Hadoop cluster.

questions.question_text: PySpark is:
choices: The Python API for Apache Spark
questions.correct_answer: The Python API for Apache Spark
questions.explanation: PySpark lets you write Spark jobs in Python.

questions.question_text: spark.read.parquet('path') in PySpark:
choices: Reads a Parquet file into a Spark DataFrame
questions.correct_answer: Reads a Parquet file into a Spark DataFrame
questions.explanation: PySpark can read Parquet, CSV, JSON, Delta, and many other formats.

questions.question_text: Spark can run on Azure Databricks, Azure Synapse, and Amazon EMR.
questions.explanation: Spark is cloud-agnostic — it runs on all major cloud platforms as a managed service.

questions.question_text: The Catalyst Optimizer in Spark:
choices: Optimises the logical and physical execution plan for DataFrame/SQL queries
questions.correct_answer: Optimises the logical and physical execution plan for DataFrame/SQL queries
questions.explanation: Catalyst analyses and rewrites query plans for maximum efficiency before execution.

questions.question_text: To avoid data skew in Spark joins you can:
choices: Salting the skewed key or broadcast joining the smaller table
questions.correct_answer: Salting the skewed key or broadcast joining the smaller table
questions.explanation: Broadcast join avoids shuffle entirely for small tables; salting distributes skewed keys evenly.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?
choices: List is mutable (can be changed); tuple is immutable (cannot be changed after creation)
Tuple is mutable; list is immutable
questions.correct_answer: List is mutable (can be changed); tuple is immutable (cannot be changed after creation)
questions.explanation: Use tuples for fixed data (coordinates, DB records); lists for data that may change.

questions.question_text: What does *args mean in a Python function?
choices: Accepts any number of positional arguments as a tuple
questions.correct_answer: Accepts any number of positional arguments as a tuple
questions.explanation: *args collects extra positional arguments; **kwargs collects keyword arguments as a dict.

questions.question_text: What does try/except/finally do?
choices: try: run risky code; except: handle errors; finally: always runs (cleanup)
try: skip code; except: run code; finally: optional
try: loop; except: break; finally: continue
questions.correct_answer: try: run risky code; except: handle errors; finally: always runs (cleanup)
questions.explanation: finally runs regardless of success or failure — ideal for closing files or connections.

questions.question_text: What is a list comprehension?
choices: A compact way to create a list: [expression for item in iterable if condition]
A method to sort a list
questions.correct_answer: A compact way to create a list: [expression for item in iterable if condition]
questions.explanation: List comprehensions are more readable and faster than equivalent for loops.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a set and a list?
choices: Set: unordered, unique elements only; List: ordered, allows duplicates
questions.correct_answer: Set: unordered, unique elements only; List: ordered, allows duplicates
questions.explanation: Use sets for membership testing and deduplication; lists for ordered sequences.

questions.question_text: In Python, None is equivalent to 0.
questions.explanation: None is Python's null value — it is not equal to 0, False, or empty string.

questions.question_text: dict.get('key', 'default') returns:

questions.question_text: What is data profiling?
choices: Analysing data to understand its quality, structure, completeness, and relationships
questions.correct_answer: Analysing data to understand its quality, structure, completeness, and relationships
questions.explanation: Profiling is done before ETL design to understand the source data landscape.

questions.question_text: The four key dimensions of data quality are:
questions.explanation: These four dimensions cover whether data is present, unique, correct format, and coherent.

questions.question_text: A source-to-target mapping document describes:
choices: Source table/column → transformation rule → target table/column for each field
questions.correct_answer: Source table/column → transformation rule → target table/column for each field
questions.explanation: Mapping docs are the specification that ETL developers follow to build pipelines.

questions.question_text: How do you profile data for NULLs and distinct counts using SQL?
choices: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT col), SUM(CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM table
questions.correct_answer: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT col), SUM(CASE WHEN col IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM table
questions.explanation: Custom profiling queries give completeness, uniqueness, and NULL counts in one pass.

questions.question_text: When data profiling reveals quality issues, you should:
choices: Document them, raise with stakeholders, define cleansing rules, apply in ETL
questions.correct_answer: Document them, raise with stakeholders, define cleansing rules, apply in ETL
questions.explanation: Issues found in profiling become transformation requirements in the mapping document.

questions.question_text: Completeness measures the percentage of non-NULL values in a column.
questions.explanation: 100% completeness = no NULLs; 0% = all NULLs. Critical for mandatory fields.

questions.question_text: Which SQL function is used in mapping to replace a NULL source value with a default?
questions.explanation: Both handle NULLs in transformation rules in mapping documents.

questions.question_text: Referential integrity means every foreign key has a matching ___ key.
questions.explanation: FK values must match a PK in the parent table — violations are orphaned records.

questions.question_text: Data validity checks ensure:
choices: Values match expected formats, ranges, or code lists — e.g. dates are real dates
questions.correct_answer: Values match expected formats, ranges, or code lists — e.g. dates are real dates
questions.explanation: Validity is the 'is it a legal value?' check — format, range, and domain checks.

questions.question_text: A mapping document should include both the source column name and the transformation rule.
questions.explanation: Without the transformation rule, developers don't know how to convert the source to the target.

questions.question_text: Data consistency across systems means:
choices: The same entity has matching values in all systems — e.g. customer name in CRM = DW
All tables have the same number of rows
questions.correct_answer: The same entity has matching values in all systems — e.g. customer name in CRM = DW
questions.explanation: Inconsistency means the same real-world entity is represented differently across systems.

questions.question_text: To check uniqueness of a supposed primary key column:
choices: SELECT col, COUNT(*) FROM table GROUP BY col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
questions.correct_answer: SELECT col, COUNT(*) FROM table GROUP BY col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
questions.explanation: If any rows appear, the column is not unique — it cannot safely be used as a PK.

questions.question_text: A data quality score of 100% means the data is perfect for all use cases.
questions.explanation: DQ scores measure specific dimensions against defined rules — context determines what score is acceptable.

questions.question_text: UPPER(TRIM(Name)) in a mapping rule ensures:
choices: Leading/trailing spaces are removed and text is uppercased consistently
questions.correct_answer: Leading/trailing spaces are removed and text is uppercased consistently
questions.explanation: TRIM + UPPER is a common standardisation transformation in source-to-target mappings.

questions.question_text: MIN and MAX profiling on a date column helps identify:
choices: The date range of data — and whether future or past dates exist that seem wrong
questions.correct_answer: The date range of data — and whether future or past dates exist that seem wrong
questions.explanation: Dates outside expected ranges (e.g. year 1900 or 2099) indicate data quality issues.

questions.question_text: What are the three levels of data modelling?
choices: Conceptual (high-level entities), Logical (attributes and keys), Physical (database objects)
questions.correct_answer: Conceptual (high-level entities), Logical (attributes and keys), Physical (database objects)
questions.explanation: Each level adds more technical detail — Conceptual for business, Physical for implementation.

questions.question_text: First Normal Form (1NF) requires:
choices: Atomic values only — no repeating groups, no multi-valued columns, each row unique
questions.correct_answer: Atomic values only — no repeating groups, no multi-valued columns, each row unique
questions.explanation: 1NF eliminates repeating groups — e.g. no Phone1, Phone2, Phone3 columns.

questions.question_text: 2NF adds to 1NF by requiring:
choices: No partial dependencies — non-key columns must depend on the WHOLE primary key
questions.correct_answer: No partial dependencies — non-key columns must depend on the WHOLE primary key
questions.explanation: 2NF matters only for composite PKs — every non-key column must need ALL key columns.

questions.question_text: 3NF adds to 2NF by requiring:
choices: No transitive dependencies — non-key columns must depend only on the PK, not each other
questions.correct_answer: No transitive dependencies — non-key columns must depend only on the PK, not each other
questions.explanation: 3NF removes columns that depend on other non-key columns rather than directly on the PK.

questions.question_text: When would you deliberately denormalise a model?
choices: In reporting/DW layers to improve read performance by reducing joins
questions.correct_answer: In reporting/DW layers to improve read performance by reducing joins
questions.explanation: Denormalisation trades storage efficiency for query speed — standard in data warehouses.

questions.question_text: A foreign key in a child table must reference a primary key in the parent table.
questions.explanation: This is referential integrity — the FK value must exist as a PK in the referenced table.

questions.question_text: ER diagrams use crow's foot notation to show:
choices: The cardinality of relationships — one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many
questions.correct_answer: The cardinality of relationships — one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many
questions.explanation: Crow's foot symbols indicate how many instances of one entity relate to another.

questions.question_text: A surrogate key is an artificially generated ___ used as a primary key instead of a natural key.
questions.explanation: Surrogate keys (e.g. INT IDENTITY) are stable and independent of business data.

questions.question_text: Many-to-many relationships in a relational database are resolved by:
choices: Creating a junction/bridge table with foreign keys to both entities
Adding multiple foreign keys to one table
questions.correct_answer: Creating a junction/bridge table with foreign keys to both entities
questions.explanation: A bridge table breaks a M:M into two 1:M relationships — e.g. StudentCourse table.

questions.question_text: Physical data models include table names, data types, indexes, and constraints.
questions.explanation: Physical models are implementation-ready — they match the actual database objects.

questions.question_text: A natural key is:
choices: A key derived from the business data itself — e.g. National Insurance Number
questions.correct_answer: A key derived from the business data itself — e.g. National Insurance Number
questions.explanation: Natural keys have business meaning; surrogate keys are arbitrary system-generated IDs.

questions.question_text: Normalisation primarily helps with:
choices: Eliminating data redundancy and preventing update/insert/delete anomalies
questions.correct_answer: Eliminating data redundancy and preventing update/insert/delete anomalies
questions.explanation: Anomalies occur when the same data is stored multiple times — normalisation prevents this.

questions.question_text: A conceptual model includes column data types.
questions.explanation: Data types appear in the Physical model — the conceptual model shows only entities and relationships.

questions.question_text: BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) is:
choices: A stricter version of 3NF that handles certain edge cases with overlapping candidate keys
questions.correct_answer: A stricter version of 3NF that handles certain edge cases with overlapping candidate keys
questions.explanation: BCNF is rarely needed in practice but appears in database theory questions.

questions.question_text: Index a column when:
choices: It is frequently used in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY clauses and the table is large
questions.correct_answer: It is frequently used in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY clauses and the table is large
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but slow writes — choose carefully based on query patterns.

questions.question_text: What is data lineage?
choices: Tracking the origin, movement, transformation, and consumption of data end-to-end
questions.correct_answer: Tracking the origin, movement, transformation, and consumption of data end-to-end
questions.explanation: Lineage answers: where did this data come from, what happened to it, where did it go?

questions.question_text: The DAMA framework covers how many knowledge areas?
questions.explanation: DAMA-DMBOK2 defines 11 data management knowledge areas including Data Quality and Governance.

questions.question_text: A Data Steward is responsible for:
choices: Data quality, definitions, and governance within a specific business domain
questions.correct_answer: Data quality, definitions, and governance within a specific business domain
questions.explanation: Data Stewards are business-facing roles — they own data quality accountability in their domain.

questions.question_text: Technical Metadata vs Business Metadata:
choices: Technical: schema, data types, table sizes; Business: definitions, KPI formulas, ownership
Business metadata is stored in system catalogues
Technical metadata is for business users
questions.correct_answer: Technical: schema, data types, table sizes; Business: definitions, KPI formulas, ownership
questions.explanation: Technical metadata lives in system catalogues; business metadata lives in data catalogues.

questions.question_text: Microsoft Purview is used for:
choices: Data governance, cataloguing, lineage tracking, and sensitivity classification across Azure
questions.correct_answer: Data governance, cataloguing, lineage tracking, and sensitivity classification across Azure
questions.explanation: Microsoft Purview is the Azure data governance and cataloguing service.

questions.question_text: Data lineage helps with impact analysis — understanding what breaks if a source column changes.
questions.explanation: Lineage maps dependencies so you can predict the downstream impact of any upstream change.

questions.question_text: A Data Owner differs from a Data Steward in that the Data Owner:
choices: Is accountable for the data asset and approves access policies
Does the day-to-day data quality work
questions.correct_answer: Is accountable for the data asset and approves access policies
questions.explanation: Owner = accountability and authority; Steward = day-to-day data quality management.

questions.question_text: A data ___ is a central inventory of data assets with metadata, lineage, and governance information.
questions.explanation: A data catalogue like Microsoft Purview enables data discovery and governance at scale.

questions.question_text: Data quality rules in a pipeline are used to:
choices: Detect and flag bad data before it enters the target system
questions.correct_answer: Detect and flag bad data before it enters the target system
questions.explanation: Quality checks in ETL catch issues at load time rather than after the fact.

questions.question_text: Operational metadata includes information about ETL job run times, row counts, and errors.
questions.explanation: Operational metadata tracks the ETL pipeline's performance and behaviour over time.

questions.question_text: A data glossary provides:
choices: Agreed business definitions for data terms — e.g. what 'Active Customer' means
questions.correct_answer: Agreed business definitions for data terms — e.g. what 'Active Customer' means
questions.explanation: Without agreed definitions, different teams calculate the same metric differently.

questions.question_text: GDPR impacts data governance by requiring:
choices: Data privacy, right to erasure, consent tracking, and knowing where personal data is stored
questions.correct_answer: Data privacy, right to erasure, consent tracking, and knowing where personal data is stored
questions.explanation: GDPR compliance requires full lineage of personal data and the ability to delete it on request.

questions.question_text: Data lineage can be tracked automatically by tools like Microsoft Purview when connected to ADF.
questions.explanation: Purview auto-discovers lineage from ADF pipelines, Synapse, and other connected services.

questions.question_text: The 'right to erasure' under GDPR means:
choices: An individual can request their personal data be deleted from all systems
Companies must delete all data after 1 year
ETL logs must be cleared weekly
questions.correct_answer: An individual can request their personal data be deleted from all systems
questions.explanation: Right to erasure (right to be forgotten) requires knowing exactly where personal data exists.

questions.question_text: Which best describes a data governance framework?
choices: A set of policies, roles, processes, and standards to manage data as a strategic asset
questions.correct_answer: A set of policies, roles, processes, and standards to manage data as a strategic asset
questions.explanation: Governance is the organisational structure and rules for managing data across the enterprise.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between a BRD and an FSD?
choices: BRD: WHAT the business needs (business language); FSD: HOW the system will meet it (technical detail)
questions.correct_answer: BRD: WHAT the business needs (business language); FSD: HOW the system will meet it (technical detail)
questions.explanation: BRD captures requirements; FSD specifies the solution — one feeds into the other.

questions.question_text: A gap analysis compares:
choices: AS-IS (current state) to TO-BE (desired future state) to identify what needs to change
questions.correct_answer: AS-IS (current state) to TO-BE (desired future state) to identify what needs to change
questions.explanation: Gap analysis is the foundation of requirements work — it defines the scope of change.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between UAT and SIT?
choices: SIT: technical team tests system integrations; UAT: business users test against acceptance criteria
questions.correct_answer: SIT: technical team tests system integrations; UAT: business users test against acceptance criteria
questions.explanation: SIT validates technical integration; UAT validates business requirements are met.

questions.question_text: A swimlane diagram shows:
choices: Who does what in a process — each lane represents a role or system with their activities
questions.correct_answer: Who does what in a process — each lane represents a role or system with their activities
questions.explanation: Swimlanes visualise handoffs between people or systems — ideal for process mapping.

questions.question_text: How do you translate business requirements into data requirements?
choices: Identify what data is needed, from where, in what format, at what granularity, and how often
questions.correct_answer: Identify what data is needed, from where, in what format, at what granularity, and how often
questions.explanation: Data requirements bridge business needs and technical implementation of data pipelines.

questions.question_text: A BRD should contain technical implementation details like SQL queries.
questions.explanation: BRD is written in business language — technical details belong in the FSD or design documents.

questions.question_text: Requirements elicitation techniques include:
choices: Workshops, interviews, surveys, observation, document analysis
questions.correct_answer: Workshops, interviews, surveys, observation, document analysis
questions.explanation: BSAs use multiple techniques to surface explicit and implicit requirements from stakeholders.

questions.question_text: UAT sign-off means business users ___ the system meets their requirements.
questions.explanation: UAT sign-off is formal approval that the delivered system meets business acceptance criteria.

questions.question_text: Change management during a project involves:
choices: Controlling scope changes through a formal change request process
questions.correct_answer: Controlling scope changes through a formal change request process
questions.explanation: Without change control, scope creep derails timelines and budgets.

questions.question_text: SIT is performed by business users to validate the system meets their needs.
questions.explanation: SIT is a technical testing phase done by the IT/QA team — UAT is done by business users.

questions.question_text: A use case describes:
choices: A specific way a user interacts with a system to achieve a goal
questions.correct_answer: A specific way a user interacts with a system to achieve a goal
questions.explanation: Use cases capture functional requirements from the user's perspective.

questions.question_text: RACI in project management stands for:
questions.explanation: RACI defines who does the work, who owns the outcome, who advises, and who is kept in the loop.

questions.question_text: A BSA needs to understand both business processes and data systems to be effective.
questions.explanation: BSAs bridge business and IT — understanding both domains is core to the role.

questions.question_text: Acceptance criteria in UAT are:
choices: Specific, measurable conditions the system must meet for stakeholders to approve it
questions.correct_answer: Specific, measurable conditions the system must meet for stakeholders to approve it
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are the measurable yardstick against which UAT is executed.

questions.question_text: Process mapping helps a BSA to:
choices: Visualise current state, identify inefficiencies, and define the improved future state
questions.correct_answer: Visualise current state, identify inefficiencies, and define the improved future state
questions.explanation: Process maps are the foundation for gap analysis and requirements gathering.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: Explain the difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK().
choices: RANK() skips numbers after a tie; DENSE_RANK() assigns the same rank but never skips
questions.correct_answer: RANK() skips numbers after a tie; DENSE_RANK() assigns the same rank but never skips
questions.explanation: Classic interview answer — know both behaviours and be ready to write an example.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: How do you find the second highest salary in a table?
choices: SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees)
SELECT TOP 2 Salary FROM Employees ORDER BY Salary DESC
SELECT RANK() FROM Employees WHERE Rank = 2
questions.correct_answer: SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees)
questions.explanation: Correlated subquery approach works without window functions and is a common interview question.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: What causes a query to run slowly on a large table?
choices: Missing indexes, table scans, non-SARGable predicates (functions on indexed columns), large joins
questions.correct_answer: Missing indexes, table scans, non-SARGable predicates (functions on indexed columns), large joins
questions.explanation: Performance questions test whether you understand query optimisation fundamentals.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: Explain SCD Type 2 and when you would use it.
choices: Add a new row with StartDate, EndDate, IsCurrent — used when you need full history of changes
Overwrite the old value — used for all changes
Add a PreviousValue column — used for current and one prior state
Delete the old record — used for GDPR compliance
questions.correct_answer: Add a new row with StartDate, EndDate, IsCurrent — used when you need full history of changes
questions.explanation: Type 2 is the most important SCD type — interviewers test this in every DW interview.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
choices: ETL transforms before loading (SSIS on-prem); ELT loads raw then transforms in the target (ADF/Databricks cloud)
ETL is only used in the cloud
questions.correct_answer: ETL transforms before loading (SSIS on-prem); ELT loads raw then transforms in the target (ADF/Databricks cloud)
questions.explanation: ETL vs ELT is a standard interview topic — tie your answer to the tools you use.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: What is the grain of a fact table?
choices: The level of detail each row represents — must be defined before designing the fact table
The size of the table in GB
questions.correct_answer: The level of detail each row represents — must be defined before designing the fact table
questions.explanation: Grain definition ensures consistency — all measures in the fact must be at the same granularity.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: What is the difference between the Merge and Merge Join transformations in SSIS?
choices: Merge combines two sorted streams (union); Merge Join joins two sorted streams (like SQL JOIN)
questions.correct_answer: Merge combines two sorted streams (union); Merge Join joins two sorted streams (like SQL JOIN)
questions.explanation: This is a classic SSIS interview trap — the names suggest they are similar but they do very different things.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: What does CALCULATE do in DAX?
choices: Evaluates an expression in a modified filter context — the most powerful DAX function
questions.correct_answer: Evaluates an expression in a modified filter context — the most powerful DAX function
questions.explanation: CALCULATE is asked in almost every Power BI interview — know it inside out.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: When would you use ADF over SSIS?
choices: ADF for cloud-native, serverless, 90+ connectors; SSIS for complex on-prem transformations with rich transforms
They do exactly the same thing
questions.correct_answer: ADF for cloud-native, serverless, 90+ connectors; SSIS for complex on-prem transformations with rich transforms
questions.explanation: Knowing when to use which tool shows architectural awareness — a key senior analyst skill.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: What is the difference between Pandas merge and PySpark join?
choices: Pandas merge runs on one machine (single node); PySpark join runs distributed across a cluster
PySpark merge is faster on small data
questions.correct_answer: Pandas merge runs on one machine (single node); PySpark join runs distributed across a cluster
questions.explanation: Scale is the key differentiator — Pandas for data that fits in memory; PySpark for big data.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: How would you ensure data quality in an ETL pipeline?
choices: Profile source data, define DQ rules, add validation checks in the pipeline, log and alert on failures, reconcile counts and sums
questions.correct_answer: Profile source data, define DQ rules, add validation checks in the pipeline, log and alert on failures, reconcile counts and sums
questions.explanation: A structured DQ approach demonstrates maturity — this answer covers the full lifecycle.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: How do you handle conflicting requirements from different stakeholders?
choices: Facilitate a meeting to clarify priorities, document the conflict, escalate to sponsor if needed, agree a resolution
questions.correct_answer: Facilitate a meeting to clarify priorities, document the conflict, escalate to sponsor if needed, agree a resolution
questions.explanation: Conflict resolution is a core BSA skill — structured facilitation and documentation are key.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: Walk me through how you would validate a data warehouse load.
choices: 1) Count rows source vs target  2) SUM key measures  3) Check for NULLs on mandatory fields  4) Sample spot checks  5) Compare to previous load
questions.correct_answer: 1) Count rows source vs target  2) SUM key measures  3) Check for NULLs on mandatory fields  4) Sample spot checks  5) Compare to previous load
questions.explanation: A structured validation approach is what experienced data professionals do — show the steps.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: Describe the Medallion Architecture.
choices: Bronze (raw) → Silver (cleaned) → Gold (business-ready) — progressively refining data quality in a Lakehouse
questions.correct_answer: Bronze (raw) → Silver (cleaned) → Gold (business-ready) — progressively refining data quality in a Lakehouse
questions.explanation: Medallion is the standard Lakehouse architecture — expected knowledge for Azure data roles.

questions.question_text: Interview Q: What is Delta Lake and why is it used?
choices: Open table format on ADLS with ACID transactions, time travel, schema enforcement, and upsert support
A lake in the Azure cloud
questions.correct_answer: Open table format on ADLS with ACID transactions, time travel, schema enforcement, and upsert support
questions.explanation: Delta Lake solves reliability issues with raw Parquet/CSV on data lakes — essential Azure knowledge.

questions.question_text: Where in SSMS do you write a CTE?
choices: In the Stored Procedures node only
In any Query Editor window — CTEs are written inline before the main SELECT
questions.correct_answer: In any Query Editor window — CTEs are written inline before the main SELECT
questions.explanation: CTEs are part of a T-SQL statement and written in the query editor, not stored separately.

questions.question_text: You created a #temp table in one query window. Can you see it in a second new query window in SSMS?
choices: Yes, all windows share temp tables
No — #temp tables are session-scoped; a new window is a new session
Yes if you use the same login
questions.correct_answer: No — #temp tables are session-scoped; a new window is a new session
questions.explanation: Each SSMS query window has its own session. #temp tables are not visible across sessions.

questions.question_text: Where do you see temporary tables listed in SSMS Object Explorer?
choices: Under System Databases > tempdb > Temporary Tables
They are invisible in Object Explorer
questions.correct_answer: Under System Databases > tempdb > Temporary Tables
questions.explanation: Temp tables live in tempdb and appear there in Object Explorer while the session is active.

questions.question_text: How do you explicitly drop a temp table before recreating it in the same script?
questions.explanation: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS avoids errors if the table doesn't exist yet — safe to use at the top of scripts.

questions.question_text: A CTE is defined using which keyword at the start?
questions.explanation: Syntax: WITH cte_name AS (SELECT ...) SELECT * FROM cte_name;

questions.question_text: In SSMS, if you get the error 'Invalid object name #MyTemp', what is the most likely cause?
choices: The table was created in a different session or was already dropped
You need to prefix it with dbo.
Temp tables require a special permission
The table name has too many characters
questions.correct_answer: The table was created in a different session or was already dropped
questions.explanation: #temp tables are session-scoped and auto-drop when the session ends.

questions.question_text: How do you run only part of a script in SSMS — for example, just the CTE section?
choices: Highlight the text you want to run, then press F5
SSMS always runs the full script
questions.correct_answer: Highlight the text you want to run, then press F5
questions.explanation: Selecting text before F5 restricts execution to that selection.

questions.question_text: How do you add a comment explaining a CTE in T-SQL?
choices: /* This is a comment */ or -- single line comment
questions.correct_answer: /* This is a comment */ or -- single line comment
questions.explanation: T-SQL uses -- for single-line and /* */ for multi-line comments.

questions.question_text: What SSMS keyboard shortcut formats/indents selected SQL code?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+K then Ctrl+F auto-formats the selected SQL in SSMS.

questions.question_text: To check whether a temp table already exists before creating it, which pattern do you use?
choices: IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tempdb.sys.objects WHERE name LIKE '#MyTemp%') DROP TABLE #MyTemp
questions.correct_answer: IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tempdb.sys.objects WHERE name LIKE '#MyTemp%') DROP TABLE #MyTemp
questions.explanation: This checks tempdb system tables for the temp table before dropping.

questions.question_text: Where does a recursive CTE require the MAXRECURSION option to be set if depth exceeds 100?
choices: As a query hint OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) at the end of the final SELECT
questions.correct_answer: As a query hint OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) at the end of the final SELECT
questions.explanation: Add OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0) after the final SELECT to allow unlimited recursion.

questions.question_text: In SSMS, what colour does SSMS highlight SQL keywords like WITH, SELECT, FROM in by default?
questions.explanation: SSMS syntax highlights reserved keywords in blue by default.

questions.question_text: A CTE result can be referenced multiple times in the same query after its WITH block.
questions.explanation: You can SELECT from a CTE as many times as needed within the same query.

questions.question_text: Pressing Ctrl+Z in SSMS undoes changes to the query text in the editor.
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Z is standard undo in the SSMS query editor.

questions.question_text: In Python, how do you create a variable to hold a customer's name?
questions.explanation: Python uses a simple `name = value` assignment. No type keyword, no DIM, no semicolons needed. The variable's type is inferred from the value.

questions.question_text: Python requires you to declare a variable's type (like INTEGER or VARCHAR) before using it, similar to a SQL column definition.
questions.explanation: Python is dynamically typed. You just assign a value and Python figures out the type. This differs from SQL DDL where you declare column types up front.

questions.question_text:
What does this code print?

price = 100
tax = 0.2
print(price * (1 + tax))
questions.explanation: Multiplying an int (100) by a float (1.2) gives a float, so the result is 120.0. Mixing int and float always produces a float.

questions.question_text: The Python data type used for whole numbers like 42 is called ___.
questions.explanation: `int` is Python's whole-number type. Decimals use `float`. You can check any value's type with the built-in type() function.

questions.question_text: Which value is a Python string (text)?
questions.explanation: Text wrapped in single or double quotes is a string (str). Numbers and True/False are not strings. Think of str like a VARCHAR column.

questions.question_text: What is the boolean (True/False) data type best compared to in your banking work?
choices: A yes/no or flag column (e.g. is_active)
questions.correct_answer: A yes/no or flag column (e.g. is_active)
questions.explanation: Python's bool holds only True or False, just like a boolean/flag column (is_active, is_fraud) in a database.

questions.question_text:
What does this print?

x = "5"
y = 3
print(x + y)
choices: A TypeError (cannot add str and int)
questions.correct_answer: A TypeError (cannot add str and int)
questions.explanation: x is the string "5", not the number 5. Python will not silently mix text and numbers, so adding them raises a TypeError. You'd convert first with int(x).

questions.question_text: To convert the string "42" into the number 42, you wrap it in the ___() function.
questions.explanation: int("42") converts text to a whole number. Similarly float("3.14") makes a decimal and str(42) makes text. This is called type casting/conversion.

questions.question_text:
What does this print?

name = "Ada"
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
questions.explanation: An f-string (the f before the quote) lets you insert a variable inside {curly braces}. It's the modern, readable way to build text in Python.

questions.explanation: df.info() lists columns, non-null counts, and data types. df.dtypes shows just types, and df.columns lists names. All are quick data-quality checks.

questions.question_text: Combining two DataFrames on a shared key column (like joining tables) is done with which method?
questions.explanation: pd.merge(df1, df2, on="id") joins DataFrames on a key, just like a SQL JOIN. You can specify inner, left, right, or outer joins via the `how` argument.

questions.question_text:
What does this print?

import numpy as np
prices = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(prices.mean())
questions.explanation: NumPy's .mean() averages the array: (10+20+30)/3 = 20.0. NumPy arrays come with fast built-in statistics methods.

Which statement best answers this?
choices: pandas/NumPy use vectorized operations in optimized C code, processing whole columns at once - far faster and more concise than Python loops over each row.

lessons.lesson_name: APIs, JSON & Calling an LLM from Python

questions.question_text: What is an API, in plain terms?
choices: A defined way for two programs to request and exchange data
questions.correct_answer: A defined way for two programs to request and exchange data
questions.explanation: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a contract for software to talk to software - like a service window where you send a request and get a response.

questions.question_text: JSON is a common text format for sending structured data between systems.
questions.explanation: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) uses key-value pairs and lists. It's the standard data format for most web APIs, including LLM APIs.

questions.question_text: JSON's structure of {"key": "value"} pairs maps most naturally to which Python type?
questions.explanation: JSON objects become Python dicts, and JSON arrays become Python lists. This near-perfect match makes JSON easy to work with in Python.

questions.question_text: The popular Python library for making HTTP requests to APIs is called ___.
questions.explanation: The `requests` library makes calling APIs simple: requests.get(url) or requests.post(url, json=...). It's a third-party package installed via pip.

questions.question_text: In a REST API, which HTTP method is typically used to RETRIEVE data?
questions.explanation: GET retrieves data; POST sends/creates data (used when calling an LLM with a prompt). PUT updates, DELETE removes.

questions.question_text: When you call an LLM API to send a prompt, you typically use which HTTP method?
questions.explanation: You POST your prompt and parameters in the request body (as JSON) because you're sending data for the model to process, then receive its response.

questions.question_text: An HTTP status code of 200 means the request succeeded.
questions.explanation: 200 = success. 401 = unauthorized (bad API key), 404 = not found, 429 = rate limited, 500 = server error. Checking the status code is good practice.

questions.question_text: Converting a Python dict into a JSON-formatted text string uses json.___().
questions.explanation: json.dumps() 'dumps' a Python object to a JSON string (for sending). json.loads() 'loads' a JSON string back into Python (for receiving). Remember: s = string.

questions.question_text: Where should you store your LLM API key?
choices: In an environment variable, never hardcoded in the script
Pasted directly in the code and committed to GitHub
questions.correct_answer: In an environment variable, never hardcoded in the script
questions.explanation: API keys are secrets. Store them in environment variables (or a secrets manager) and read them at runtime. Hardcoding risks leaking them in version control.

questions.question_text: Match each API concept to its meaning.

definitions: retrieve data
send data
data exchange format
credential proving who you are

questions.explanation: These four are the essentials of calling any API, including an LLM: choose a method, send/receive JSON, and authenticate with a key.

questions.question_text: Parsing a JSON string received from an API back into a Python object uses json.loads().
questions.explanation: json.loads() turns JSON text into Python dicts/lists. Many libraries also offer response.json() to do this in one step.

questions.question_text:
What does this likely retrieve?

data = response.json()
print(data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
questions.explanation: This drills into the nested JSON response to pull out the model's text. Reading an LLM reply means navigating dicts and lists by key and index.

questions.question_text: In an LLM API, the 'system' message is typically used to:
choices: Set the assistant's role, rules, and behavior
questions.correct_answer: Set the assistant's role, rules, and behavior
questions.explanation: The system message gives high-level instructions (persona, constraints). The user message holds the actual question or task.

questions.question_text: A unit of text that an LLM reads and bills by - roughly a word-piece - is called a ___.
questions.explanation: LLMs process text as tokens (chunks of characters/words). Both your prompt and the response consume tokens, which drives cost and context limits.

questions.question_text: The LLM parameter that controls randomness/creativity of the output is called ___.
questions.explanation: Lower temperature (e.g. 0) gives focused, deterministic answers - good for data extraction. Higher values add variety - useful for brainstorming.

questions.question_text: An HTTP 429 status code from an LLM API most likely means:
choices: You are being rate limited (too many requests)
questions.correct_answer: You are being rate limited (too many requests)
questions.explanation: 429 = Too Many Requests. The fix is to slow down or retry after a short wait (often with exponential backoff). 401 would mean a bad key.

questions.question_text: It is safe to commit your API key into a public GitHub repository as long as the repo has few visitors.
questions.explanation: Never commit secrets. Bots scan public repos for keys within minutes. Use environment variables and a .gitignore'd secrets file or a secrets manager.

questions.question_text:
A solution must call an LLM and may hit rate limits or timeouts. Name one practice to make those API calls robust.

Which statement best answers this?
choices: A dict gives fast lookups by key (the account number), returning the value (the record) directly - far better than scanning a list item by item.
Wrap calls in try/except, check status codes, and retry transient failures (e.g. 429/500) with backoff. This keeps automations reliable in production.
A single = assigns a value to a variable (x = 5). A double == compares two values and returns True/False (x == 5). Mixing them up is a classic beginner bug.
Functions let you write logic once and reuse it everywhere, keeping solutions readable and maintainable - a core design principle (DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself).
questions.correct_answer: Wrap calls in try/except, check status codes, and retry transient failures (e.g. 429/500) with backoff. This keeps automations reliable in production.
questions.explanation: Wrap calls in try/except, check status codes, and retry transient failures (e.g. 429/500) with backoff. This keeps automations reliable in production.

questions.question_text:
What does this code do?

import requests
r = requests.get("https://api.example.com/rates")
print(r.status_code)
choices: Calls the API and prints the HTTP status of the response
Sends a prompt to an LLM
questions.correct_answer: Calls the API and prints the HTTP status of the response
questions.explanation: requests.get() sends a GET request; r.status_code shows the result (e.g. 200). Checking it before reading r.json() avoids errors on failed calls.

questions.question_text:
In one phrase, why is JSON convenient when working with Python?

Which statement best answers this?
choices: pandas/NumPy use vectorized operations in optimized C code, processing whole columns at once - far faster and more concise than Python loops over each row.
Python variable names must start with a letter or underscore, never a digit. Valid examples: name2, _name, customer_2.

JSON objects map directly to Python dicts and JSON arrays to lists, so converting between them is trivial - making API data easy to read and manipulate.

questions.explanation: JSON objects map directly to Python dicts and JSON arrays to lists, so converting between them is trivial - making API data easy to read and manipulate.

questions.question_text: An API endpoint is best described as ___.
choices: a specific URL you send a request to for a particular function
questions.correct_answer: a specific URL you send a request to for a particular function
questions.explanation: An endpoint is the address (URL) for one API capability, e.g. /v1/messages to chat with an LLM. You send your request there and read the response.

questions.question_text: What is a Jupyter notebook best described as?
choices: A document mixing runnable code cells, output, and notes
A plain text file with no code
questions.correct_answer: A document mixing runnable code cells, output, and notes
questions.explanation: Notebooks (.ipynb) let you run code in cells and see results inline alongside notes and charts - ideal for exploring data and explaining analysis step by step.

questions.question_text: In a Jupyter notebook, cells can be run in any order, which can cause confusing state if you skip around.
questions.explanation: Because variables persist between cells, running cells out of order can produce results that don't match a clean top-to-bottom run. 'Restart & Run All' confirms reproducibility.

questions.question_text: When Python hits an error, the message printed (showing where and what went wrong) is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A traceback shows the chain of calls leading to the error and the error type/message. Read it from the bottom up - the last line names the actual error.

questions.question_text: When reading a traceback, which line usually tells you the actual error?
choices: The last line (the error type and message)
questions.correct_answer: The last line (the error type and message)
questions.explanation: The final line states the error type (e.g. KeyError) and message. The lines above trace how the code got there. Start at the bottom.

questions.question_text:
What kind of error is this?

>>> prnit("hello")
NameError: name 'prnit' is not defined
questions.explanation: A NameError means Python doesn't recognize that name - here `prnit` is a typo for `print`. Fixing the spelling resolves it.

questions.question_text: Match each common Python error to its likely cause.

definitions: malformed code (e.g. missing colon)
using an undefined/misspelled name
wrong type for an operation
missing key in a dict

questions.explanation: Recognizing the error type instantly narrows the cause: structure, a name, a type mismatch, or a missing dict key. This speeds up debugging enormously.

questions.question_text: The simplest debugging technique is adding ___() statements to see a variable's value at a given point.
questions.explanation: Sprinkling print() to inspect values is the classic, fast way to understand what code is actually doing - no special tools required.

questions.question_text:
What does this error indicate?

IndentationError: expected an indented block
choices: Code that should be indented under an if/for/def is not
questions.correct_answer: Code that should be indented under an if/for/def is not
questions.explanation: Python uses indentation to define blocks. After a line ending in a colon, the next line(s) must be indented. Mixing tabs and spaces also triggers this.

questions.question_text: Reading code top to bottom and tracing what each variable becomes is a valid way to understand an unfamiliar script.
questions.explanation: Tracing execution mentally (or with print statements) is exactly how experienced developers understand new code. You don't need to write code to read it well.
range(2) yields 0 and 1, so the loop runs twice, printing 'row 0' then 'row 1'. Tracing loop ranges is a core code-reading skill.

questions.question_text: A KeyError when accessing a dictionary means the key you asked for does not exist in that dict.
questions.explanation: d["missing"] raises KeyError if 'missing' isn't a key. Using d.get("missing") returns None instead, avoiding the crash.

questions.question_text: In a notebook, what does the number in brackets like In [5] next to a cell indicate?
choices: The order in which that cell was executed
The number of errors in the cell
The line number in the file
questions.correct_answer: The order in which that cell was executed
questions.explanation: The execution count shows the sequence cells were run in. An empty bracket [ ] means the cell hasn't run yet; * means it's still running.

questions.question_text:
What's likely wrong here?

numbers = [1, 2, 3]
print(numbers[3])
choices: IndexError - index 3 is out of range for a 3-item list
questions.correct_answer: IndexError - index 3 is out of range for a 3-item list
questions.explanation: Valid indexes are 0, 1, 2 for a 3-item list. Index 3 doesn't exist, so Python raises IndexError. The last valid index is len(list) - 1.

questions.question_text: The structure used to catch and handle errors gracefully in Python is ___ / except.
questions.explanation: A try/except block runs risky code and catches errors instead of crashing - essential for robust automations that call files or APIs.
Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError, which the except block catches, printing the friendly message instead of crashing.

questions.question_text: If you see ImportError or ModuleNotFoundError, a likely fix is to install the missing package with pip.
questions.explanation: These errors mean the library isn't available in your environment. Run `pip install <package>` (in the correct virtual environment) to fix it.

You are handed an unfamiliar Python script in a screening. Name one practical first step to understand what it does.

def greet(name):

questions.explanation: Python won't auto-mix text and numbers. Convert first: "Total: " + str(amount), or use an f-string: f"Total: {amount}".

In one phrase, why is reading code a more important skill than writing it for an AI Solutions Owner?

Which statement best answers this?

choices: which file and line number the error occurred at

lessons.lesson_name: What an LLM Is: Tokens, Parameters & Training

questions.question_text: What is a 'token' in the context of a large language model?
choices: A complete sentence the model reads at once
A chunk of text (often a word or part of a word) that the model processes as one unit
A single letter of the alphabet only
A security key used to access the model's API
questions.correct_answer: A chunk of text (often a word or part of a word) that the model processes as one unit
questions.explanation: Tokens are the units an LLM reads and writes. A token is often a word or a fragment of a word (e.g. 'banking' might be one token, 'reconciliation' might be split into several). Think of tokens like line items on a statement: the model processes them one at a time.

questions.question_text: A model's 'parameters' are best described as the learned numerical values (weights) that the model adjusts during training to capture patterns in language.
questions.explanation: Parameters are the internal weights tuned during training. More parameters generally means more capacity to store patterns, similar to how a richer rules engine can encode more business logic, though size alone does not guarantee quality.

questions.question_text: The process where a model first learns general language patterns from a very large body of text before any specialization is called ___.
questions.explanation: Pretraining is the broad, expensive phase where the model learns language from massive text. Later, fine-tuning specializes it, much like hiring a generally educated analyst and then training them on your bank's specific procedures.

questions.question_text: During pretraining, what task does a typical LLM repeatedly practice?
choices: Predicting the next token given the preceding text
Memorizing entire documents word-for-word for later recall
questions.correct_answer: Predicting the next token given the preceding text
questions.explanation: LLMs are trained on next-token prediction: given some text, guess what comes next. Repeated billions of times, this forces the model to internalize grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns. It is prediction, not lookup.

questions.question_text: A larger number of parameters always guarantees a smarter, more accurate model.
questions.explanation: Size helps capacity but is not the whole story. Data quality, training method, and fine-tuning matter enormously. A smaller, well-trained model can outperform a larger poorly-trained one, just as a small expert team can beat a large untrained one.

questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly orders the typical lifecycle of building an instruction-following LLM?
choices: Pretraining on broad text, then fine-tuning/alignment, then deployment
questions.correct_answer: Pretraining on broad text, then fine-tuning/alignment, then deployment
questions.explanation: First the model learns language broadly (pretraining), then it is shaped to follow instructions and behave safely (fine-tuning / alignment such as RLHF), then it is deployed. Each stage builds on the previous one.

questions.question_text: Match each term to its description.

definitions: A chunk of text the model processes as one unit
A learned weight adjusted during training
Broad initial learning of language from huge text
Specializing a trained model for a task or behavior

correct_answer.Token: A chunk of text the model processes as one unit
correct_answer.Parameter: A learned weight adjusted during training
correct_answer.Pretraining: Broad initial learning of language from huge text
correct_answer.Fine-tuning: Specializing a trained model for a task or behavior

questions.explanation: These four terms form the vocabulary foundation: tokens are the input units, parameters are what the model learns, pretraining is the broad phase, and fine-tuning is the specialization phase.

questions.question_text: An LLM that predicts text by estimating the most likely next token is fundamentally a ___ model.
questions.explanation: LLMs are probabilistic: they assign probabilities to possible next tokens and select among them. This is why the same prompt can yield different answers and why outputs are not guaranteed facts, only likely text.

questions.question_text: From a Business Analyst's view, why does it matter that an LLM predicts likely text rather than retrieving verified facts?
choices: It means outputs can sound confident yet be wrong, so verification controls are needed
It means the model never makes mistakes
It means the model stores a database of every fact it has seen
It means outputs are always identical for the same question
questions.correct_answer: It means outputs can sound confident yet be wrong, so verification controls are needed
questions.explanation: Because the model generates probable-sounding text, it can produce fluent but incorrect answers. As a solution owner you must design checks, citations, or human review, just as you would for an automated process that approximates rather than calculates exactly.

questions.question_text: Which statement about training data is accurate?
choices: A model only knows information that was present in its training data (up to its cutoff), plus what you give it at prompt time
A model continuously learns from every conversation in real time
A model can access any live website automatically without tools
A model's knowledge updates itself overnight
questions.correct_answer: A model only knows information that was present in its training data (up to its cutoff), plus what you give it at prompt time
questions.explanation: A base LLM is frozen after training. It does not learn from your chats and has no built-in live internet access unless connected to tools. What it 'knows' comes from training data plus whatever context you supply in the prompt.

questions.question_text: True or False: When you chat with a standard LLM, your messages permanently retrain the model so it remembers you next time.
questions.explanation: Inference (using the model) is separate from training. A standard deployed model does not update its parameters from your conversation; any 'memory' is engineered by feeding prior text back into the prompt, not by retraining.

questions.question_text: The text 'reconciliation' being broken into smaller sub-word pieces before the model reads it is an example of ___.
questions.explanation: Tokenization is the step that converts raw text into tokens. Rare or long words get split into sub-word pieces, which is why word count and token count are not the same thing.

questions.question_text:
Name two factors (besides raw parameter count) that influence how capable an LLM is.

Which statement best answers this?
choices: Capability depends on training data quality and quantity, the training method, fine-tuning and alignment (e.g. RLHF), and architecture, not just parameter count.

A system prompt centralizes rules, role, tone, and guardrails (e.g. 'never give financial advice; always cite policy'), giving consistent, auditable behavior across all user interactions, valuable for compliance.
Tokens drive both cost (you pay per token) and feasibility (content must fit the context window). Estimating tokens lets you forecast budget and judge whether a use case is even technically viable.
Attention (specifically self-attention) is the headline idea, captured in the founding paper title 'Attention Is All You Need.' If you remember one word about transformers, it is attention.
questions.correct_answer: Capability depends on training data quality and quantity, the training method, fine-tuning and alignment (e.g. RLHF), and architecture, not just parameter count.
questions.explanation: Capability depends on training data quality and quantity, the training method, fine-tuning and alignment (e.g. RLHF), and architecture, not just parameter count. This is why two models of similar size can differ widely in quality.

questions.question_text: Which analogy best captures what 'parameters' are?
choices: The dials a model tunes during training to encode patterns it has learned
The number of questions a user can ask per day
The list of countries a model can translate
The price charged per API call
questions.correct_answer: The dials a model tunes during training to encode patterns it has learned
questions.explanation: Picture millions or billions of dials; training nudges each dial so the overall model predicts text well. Those settled dial positions are the parameters (weights).

questions.question_text: A model described as having a 'knowledge cutoff' means it has no built-in awareness of events after a certain date.
questions.explanation: Because training ends at a point in time, the model's built-in knowledge stops there. For anything newer you must supply the information in the prompt or connect a retrieval/search tool.

questions.question_text: Which best distinguishes 'training' from 'inference'?
choices: Training is when the model learns its parameters; inference is when the trained model is used to generate answers
Training and inference are the same thing
Inference is when the model is built; training is when it answers questions
questions.correct_answer: Training is when the model learns its parameters; inference is when the trained model is used to generate answers
questions.explanation: Training is the (expensive, one-time-ish) learning phase that sets the weights. Inference is every time you actually run the model to get an output. As a solution owner, your ongoing costs are mostly inference.

questions.question_text: Specializing a general pretrained model on your bank's labeled examples to improve a specific task is called ___.
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning adjusts a pretrained model using a smaller, targeted dataset. It is one option for specialization, though prompting and retrieval often achieve the goal without the cost and effort of fine-tuning.

questions.question_text: Your stakeholder says 'just retrain the model overnight with today's transactions so it learns them.' What is the most accurate response?
choices: Standard models do not learn from use in real time; to use new data we supply it at prompt time or run a deliberate fine-tuning/retraining project
Yes, the model automatically absorbs all new data each night
We simply ask the model to remember and it permanently does
Retraining a large model is instant and free
questions.correct_answer: Standard models do not learn from use in real time; to use new data we supply it at prompt time or run a deliberate fine-tuning/retraining project
questions.explanation: This tests the training-vs-inference distinction in a realistic scenario. Models do not self-update from usage. New information is delivered via the prompt (context/retrieval) or through an intentional, resource-intensive training effort.

questions.question_text: Why can two different prompts containing the same number of words produce different token counts?
choices: Because tokenization splits text by sub-word pieces, so word length and rarity change the token count
Because the model counts only nouns
Because longer words always equal exactly one token
questions.correct_answer: Because tokenization splits text by sub-word pieces, so word length and rarity change the token count
questions.explanation: Common short words may be a single token while long or rare words split into several. So token count, which drives cost and limits, does not map one-to-one to word count.

questions.question_text:
In one sentence, explain what an LLM fundamentally does when it generates a response.

Which statement best answers this?
choices: At its core, an LLM repeatedly predicts the most probable next token given everything so far, stringing those predictions together into a fluent response.
Attention lets the model relate words to each other and focus on the most relevant ones for the current prediction. That relevance-weighting is the heart of the transformer.
Beyond raw capability: cost, latency/speed, context window size, data privacy and residency, compliance, deployment model, and vendor reliability all shape the decision.
More examples improve guidance and consistency but consume more tokens, raising cost and eating into the limited context window. Balancing the two is a core solution-design judgment call.
questions.correct_answer: At its core, an LLM repeatedly predicts the most probable next token given everything so far, stringing those predictions together into a fluent response.
questions.explanation: At its core, an LLM repeatedly predicts the most probable next token given everything so far, stringing those predictions together into a fluent response. Keep this mental model: it is sophisticated pattern-based prediction, not fact retrieval.

questions.question_text: Match each phase of an LLM's life to what mainly drives its cost.

definitions: Huge one-time compute over massive datasets
Smaller targeted training on curated examples
Ongoing per-request cost every time the model is used

correct_answer.Pretraining: Huge one-time compute over massive datasets
correct_answer.Fine-tuning: Smaller targeted training on curated examples
correct_answer.Inference: Ongoing per-request cost every time the model is used

questions.explanation: Knowing where cost lives helps you budget. Pretraining is a massive upfront expense (usually borne by the model vendor), fine-tuning is a smaller project cost, and inference is your recurring operational cost as a solution owner.

lessons.lesson_name: Inside the Model: Transformers & Attention (conceptual only)

questions.question_text: What is the 'transformer' in the context of modern LLMs?
choices: The neural network architecture that underpins most modern LLMs
A tool that converts PDFs into text
The electrical component that powers the data center
questions.correct_answer: The neural network architecture that underpins most modern LLMs
questions.explanation: The transformer (introduced in 2017) is the model design behind GPT, Claude, Gemini and others. You do not need to build one, but knowing the name and that 'attention' is its key idea is essential for technical conversations.

questions.question_text: The mechanism that lets a transformer weigh how much each token should 'pay attention to' other tokens in the input is called ___.
questions.explanation: Attention lets the model decide which earlier words are most relevant to interpret the current word. For example, linking 'it' back to the right noun. It is the defining innovation of the transformer.

questions.question_text: Conceptually, what problem does the attention mechanism solve?
choices: It helps the model capture relationships between words even when they are far apart in the text
It compresses files to save disk space
questions.correct_answer: It helps the model capture relationships between words even when they are far apart in the text
questions.explanation: Attention lets distant words influence each other, so the model understands context and long-range dependencies. Like an analyst cross-referencing a clause on page 1 with a definition on page 30.

questions.question_text: Transformers process the tokens of a prompt largely in parallel rather than strictly one-by-one in sequence.
questions.explanation: Unlike older sequential models, transformers can process tokens in parallel, which is a big reason they scale to huge datasets efficiently. This parallelism was a key practical breakthrough.

questions.question_text: Since transformers process tokens in parallel and have no inherent sense of word order, they add ___ information so the model knows each token's place in the sequence.
questions.explanation: Positional encoding injects order information. Without it, 'the bank approved the loan' and 'the loan approved the bank' would look identical to the model. Order matters, so position must be encoded.

questions.question_text: True or False: Understanding the exact matrix math inside attention is required for a solutions owner to scope LLM projects effectively.
questions.explanation: Conceptual fluency is the goal. You need to explain what attention does (relate tokens to each other based on relevance) and why it matters, not derive the math. Leave the internals to model engineers.

questions.question_text: Match each transformer concept to its plain-language role.
